opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think LLM training is almost uniquely well suited to this, and it comes down to a few properties that line up really nicely.

The first is that you have a very clean objective. Most of the time you're looking at something like validation loss, or some eval metric, and it's just a number. It goes down or it goes up. You don't need a human in the loop to squint at it and decide whether things got better. That's huge, because the moment you need human judgment at every step, the loop slows to human speed.

The second is that the whole thing lives in code. The model, the data pipeline, the optimizer, the hyperparameters: it's all just a repository. So an agent can read it, form a hypothesis like "maybe the learning rate schedule is off" or "let's try a different initialization," make an edit, kick off a run, and look at the result. The action space is literally editing text files, which is exactly what these models are already good at.

Third, you can make the experiments small. You don't have to train a frontier model to learn something. You can set up a little training run that takes five or ten minutes on a single GPU, and a lot of what you find there transfers, at least directionally. So you get a fast feedback cycle: try something, measure, keep it or revert it, repeat. Overnight, an agent can run a hundred experiments, which is more than a person might do in weeks.

And honestly, a lot of what a researcher does day to day in this setting is fairly mechanical. You tweak something, you watch the loss curve, you go "huh, that helped a little," you commit it. It's search with some intuition sprinkled on top. The agents are getting decent at the intuition part, and they're tireless at the search part.

So when you put it together, it's a closed loop: clear metric, everything is code, cheap and fast experiments, and a lot of incremental hill climbing. That's kind of the ideal sandbox for autonomy. I don't think it replaces the big conceptual leaps yet. But for squeezing out the next ten percent, it's surprisingly effective, and it's a little humbling to watch it find things you missed.

r001.rationale: It describes optimizing validation loss or an eval metric, but does not predict that the loop will overfit to those metrics.

r002.rationale: It proposes running experiments and measuring results, but does not suggest having the system devise additional evaluation metrics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that makes LLM training kind of special, in my mind, is that it's one of the most legible optimization problems we have. You have a single scalar, the loss, and almost everything about the system ultimately gets scored by that number. And it's a very reliable signal. In a lot of software engineering, you make a change and the question of "was that better" is fuzzy, it depends on taste, it depends on who you ask. In training, you run the experiment, you look at the validation loss or a few downstream evals, and you get an answer. That's exactly the kind of environment where an autonomous loop can actually make progress, because the reward is clean.

The second thing is that the search space is huge and mostly unexplored. If you look at a training run, there are hundreds of knobs. Learning rate schedules, batch size, weight decay, the exact shape of the architecture, data mixtures, all the little tricks in the optimizer. Humans have only tried a tiny fraction of the combinations, and the ones we have tried were mostly set by someone's intuition and then never revisited because it's expensive and boring to sweep. An agent doesn't get bored. It can run the experiment, read the result, form a hypothesis, modify the code, run it again, and just keep going overnight, for weeks, in parallel.

And the third piece, which I think people underrate, is that the whole thing is just code. The entire training stack for a small model can fit in a few files. That means the agent isn't working against some giant opaque system, it can actually read the whole thing, understand it, and make targeted edits. So you get this nice property where the object being optimized is small and legible, the reward is measurable, and the experiments are reproducible. That's basically the ideal setup for a loop that proposes, tests, and keeps what works.

Now, the caveat is that the loop is only as good as your eval. If the agent is optimizing the wrong metric it will happily find clever ways to game it, and you'll end up with something that looks great on your dashboard and is worse in practice. So a lot of the real work ends up being on the human side, in deciding what you're actually measuring. But given a decent metric, I think this is one of the clearest places where you can let the model do the research and get real wins.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent optimizing the wrong metric will find ways to game it, producing strong dashboard results but worse real-world performance.

r002.rationale: It assigns metric selection to humans; it does not propose having the autonomous system devise additional evaluation metrics.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you have a very clear, measurable objective. You make a change to the training code, run an experiment, and look at the validation loss. Did it get better? How much compute did you use? That gives you a feedback loop that’s relatively easy to automate.

And a lot of the work already looks like that. A researcher has an idea, modifies the architecture or the optimizer or the data mixture, launches a run, and interprets the result. An LLM can potentially do more and more of that loop, because the thing it’s manipulating is code and the feedback is quantitative.

The catch is that experiments are expensive, so you need to be smart about which ones you run. And improving a small model doesn’t necessarily mean the same change will help at scale. But you can imagine an agent running small experiments, keeping track of what worked, and using that evidence to decide what deserves a bigger run. It’s a fairly concrete setting for autonomy: you have an environment, actions you can take, and a signal telling you whether you’re making progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes optimizing validation loss and choosing experiments, but does not predict that the loop will overfit to its optimized metrics.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose having the optimization system devise additional evaluation metrics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing is that you have a very clear, measurable objective. You make a change to the training code, run an experiment, and look at the validation loss. Did it go down? How much compute did you spend getting there? That gives you a fairly clean feedback loop.

And a lot of the work is already happening inside a computer. You’re changing an optimizer, a learning-rate schedule, the architecture, how you mix the data. An agent can propose a change, launch the run, inspect the results, and decide what to try next. It doesn’t have to interact with the physical world.

The catch is that experiments can be expensive, and the feedback can be noisy. So the interesting problem becomes: can the agent design small experiments that actually teach it something, and can it tell which improvements will survive at a larger scale? But the basic structure is very appealing. You have an environment, you have actions, and you have a score. You can close the loop.

r001.rationale: The response describes optimizing validation loss and notes noisy feedback and scale transfer, but it does not predict that the loop will overfit to its chosen metrics.

r002.rationale: It suggests the agent design small experiments, but does not propose having the optimization system devise additional evaluation metrics.
